title: Assume co-responsibility and participation in human resource management

lessons.title: Workforce planning, recruitment and induction
lessons.html:
Shared responsibility for people

On most farms there is no large HR department. Farm managers, supervisors and team leaders share responsibility for human resource management with the owner or HR officer. At NQF level 4 you participate in planning staff needs, recruitment, induction, performance management, training and labour relations, always within farm policy and labour law.

Workforce planning

  • Use the production calendar to estimate labour needs per month: permanent, seasonal and contract.
  • Identify skills required: tractor drivers, spray operators, irrigators, pickers, packers, team leaders.
  • Plan for peaks such as harvest and for succession when key staff retire or leave.
  • Consider labour costs in the budget, including the current national minimum wage, which is updated regularly.

Recruitment and selection

  1. Write a job description: duties, skills, hours, reporting line and pay.
  2. Advertise fairly; the Employment Equity Act 55 of 1998 prohibits unfair discrimination.
  3. Shortlist against the job requirements.
  4. Interview using the same questions for all candidates; include practical tests where relevant, such as driving a tractor safely.
  5. Check references and legal right to work; for foreign nationals, comply with immigration requirements.
  6. Issue a written contract with terms required by the Basic Conditions of Employment Act 75 of 1997.

Induction

New workers need a structured induction:

  • Farm layout, hours, pay dates, leave and payslips
  • Safety rules, PPE, emergency procedures and first aid points (OHS Act 85 of 1993)
  • Job-specific training and who to ask for help
  • Disciplinary code and grievance procedure
  • Food safety and hygiene rules where relevant

Record induction with signatures. A good start reduces accidents and staff turnover.

lessons.title: Performance, development and labour relations
lessons.html:
Performance management

  • Agree clear tasks and standards with each worker or team: quality, quantity, safety and attendance.
  • Give regular informal feedback, both praise and correction.
  • Hold periodic reviews and record outcomes.
  • Link incentives, such as piece rates or bonuses, to fair, measurable targets that do not compromise safety or quality.

Training and development

  • Identify skills gaps through observation, reviews and new technology.
  • Plan on-the-job training, mentoring and accredited training through AgriSETA-accredited providers.
  • The Skills Development Act 97 of 1998 and Skills Development Levies Act 9 of 1999 provide the framework; levy-paying employers can claim grants by submitting workplace skills plans.
  • Keep training records; some tasks such as spraying, forklift driving and first aid require certified competence.

Labour relations

  • Know the farm's disciplinary code and the Labour Relations Act 66 of 1995 requirements for fair procedure.
  • Handle minor issues promptly and consistently; record warnings.
  • For serious misconduct, follow the formal procedure: investigation, written notice, hearing with right to representation and to respond, an impartial chairperson, and a reasoned outcome.
  • Poor performance requires counselling, support and time to improve before any dismissal.
  • Respect freedom of association: workers may join trade unions.
  • Disputes may be referred to the CCMA.

Communication and worker participation

Regular team meetings, worker committees and health and safety representatives give workers a voice. Involve workers in planning tasks and solving problems; they often know the practical solutions.

Wellbeing

Support workers dealing with health issues, such as HIV and TB, substance abuse or family crises, through referral to clinics and support programmes. Keep personal information confidential.

Records

Keep accurate records of hours, leave, pay, training, incidents and discipline, as required by the BCEA and for audits.

Key points

  • Supervisors share HR responsibility within policy and law.
  • Plan labour needs from the production calendar.
  • Recruit fairly, issue written contracts and induct properly.
  • Manage performance with clear standards and feedback; train to close skills gaps.
  • Follow fair procedure in discipline and keep complete records.
